title: Arjuna's Crisis and the Undying Self
intro: Chapters 1 and 2 of the Bhagavad Gita: Arjuna's despair on the battlefield and Krishna's first teaching on the self that never dies.

posts.caption: The Bhagavad Gita, "the Song of the Lord," is a 700-verse dialogue within India's great epic, the Mahabharata. It opens with a question from the blind king Dhritarashtra to Sanjaya, who has been granted divine sight to see the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Here, the Gita one verse a day, in order, with a little context.

Two branches of one family face each other: the Kauravas, Dhritarashtra's sons, and the Pandavas, their cousins. Krishna (Madhava) has vowed not to fight and serves as charioteer to his friend Arjuna, the Pandava archer. Many scholars date the Gita's composition to roughly the 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE; tradition places the war much earlier.

Arjuna has asked Krishna to drive their chariot between the two armies so he can see whom he must fight. Krishna stops before Bhishma, the revered elder of both families, and Drona, teacher to both sides. These are Krishna's only words in chapter 1. Both sides descend from King Kuru, so "Kurus" takes in Arjuna's own family.

posts.display: Gândîva slips from my hand, and my skin burns all over, I am not able to stand, my mind is whirling.
posts.caption: Arjuna sees uncles, teachers, cousins, sons and friends in both armies, and is overcome. In the verse before, he describes his limbs failing, his mouth parched, his body trembling. Gandiva is his famous bow. Chapter 1 is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, "the yoga of Arjuna's despondency."

Arjuna's reasoning: what is a kingdom worth if the people he would share it with lie dead? Govinda, one of Krishna's names, is often explained as "protector of cows," recalling his youth among the cowherds of Vraja. Arjuna's grief is sincere, and much of the Gita is Krishna's long, patient reply to it.

Arjuna would rather die unarmed than fight his own family. In the next verse, the last of chapter 1, he sinks down in the chariot, casts aside his bow and arrows, his mind overcome with grief. The scene is set: a celebrated warrior, frozen by doubt between two armies.

Chapter 2 opens with Arjuna in tears. Krishna, called "the Blessed Lord" (Bhagavan) throughout the Gita, answers sharply: this despondency is unworthy of him. The tone will soon soften, but first Krishna tries to shake his friend awake.

Krishna's first demand is blunt: shake off this weakness of heart and stand up. Parantapa, "scorcher of foes," is one of Arjuna's many epithets. Swami Vivekananda said the whole message of the Gita lies embedded in this one verse, which he read as a call to strength and fearlessness.

This is the turning point of the whole Gita. Arjuna admits he no longer knows what dharma, right duty, requires, and asks Krishna to teach him as a disciple. From here on, a conversation between friends becomes a teaching from guru to student.

Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king, reports Arjuna's flat refusal to fight. Gudakesha ("conqueror of sleep") is Arjuna; Hrishikesha ("lord of the senses") and Govinda are Krishna. The Gita is full of such epithets, each highlighting a quality of the person named.

posts.display: Then Hrishîkesha, smiling, as it were, O Bhârata, spake these words to him, despondent, in the midst of the two armies.
posts.caption: Between the two armies, Krishna smiles. Commentators have read that half-smile in many ways: gentle reassurance, affection, or the calm of one who sees the whole picture. From the next verse on comes the heart of the Gita: Krishna's teaching.

Krishna's teaching begins here. Arjuna has been speaking like a wise man, yet grieving for what the wise do not grieve over. The next verses explain why: the real self of each person, the atman, does not die with the body.

Krishna's first argument is that the self has no beginning and no end. Schools read his "we" differently. Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita) sees here many eternal selves, distinct from one another and from God; Shankara (Advaita) says the plural refers to bodies, and that in the highest truth there is one Self.

The "dweller in the body" (dehi) passes through childhood, youth and old age, then on to another body. The Gita treats death as one more change of the same kind. Dhira, "the steadfast one," is someone whose understanding holds firm through all of them.

Matra-sparsha, "contacts of matter," means the meeting of the senses with their objects, which bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain. Their mark is that they come and go. Titiksha, the patient endurance Krishna asks for here, became one of the classic virtues of a seeker in Advaita Vedanta.

One of the Gita's most philosophical lines. Sat is what truly is and does not change; asat is what has no lasting being. Shankara's Advaita reads it as the distinction between Brahman, the one reality, and the passing world of appearances; Ramanuja reads it as the contrast between the eternal self and the perishable body.

"That" (tat) is how the Upanishads often point to ultimate reality without naming it. Commentators differ on what is meant here. Ramanuja reads it as the conscious self, subtle enough to pervade the inert matter of the body; Shankara as Brahman, which pervades everything and is one with the self.

The self is not a killer and cannot be killed: Krishna's answer to Arjuna's dread of slaying his elders. Ralph Waldo Emerson's poem "Brahma" opens with the same thought, drawing on this verse or its near-twin in the Katha Upanishad: "If the red slayer think he slays, / Or if the slain think he is slain."

Perhaps the Gita's most famous statement about the atman: unborn, eternal, ancient. This verse and the one before closely match two verses of the Katha Upanishad, where Yama, the lord of death, teaches the boy Nachiketa what survives death. There, fittingly, the teacher is Death himself.

One of the best-loved images in the Gita: the body as clothing, worn out and exchanged for new. Belief in rebirth (punarjanma) is shared by Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions, though they describe what passes from life to life very differently.

Weapons, fire, water, wind: none of the forces that destroy a body can touch the self. Krishna says this on a battlefield, with weapons all around. Verses from this passage are often recited at Hindu funerals and memorials.

Krishna turns from philosophy to plain realism: what is born will die, and in the Gita's view, what dies will be born again. If something cannot be avoided, grief cannot change it. Arjuna is mourning people who are still alive; Krishna asks him to see the whole cycle.

Beings come from the unmanifest (avyakta), appear for a while, and return to the unmanifest. A life is the visible middle of a longer story. Avyakta becomes an important word later in the Gita, especially in chapters 8 and 12.

Krishna admits the limits of words even as he teaches: the self can be wondered at, spoken of and heard about, yet still not grasped. A verse of the Katha Upanishad likewise calls both the teacher of the self and the one who comes to know it a wonder.

Krishna turns from the eternal self to svadharma, one's own duty. For Arjuna, a prince of the kshatriya (warrior) class, that means fighting a righteous war. Readings of passages like this range from literal to allegorical: Gandhi read the battle as an image of the struggle between good and evil within each person.

The argument now moves from duty to inner attitude: holding pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal. This evenness of mind is the seed of what the Gita calls yoga, which here means a discipline of action rather than physical postures.

A shift in the teaching. So far Krishna has spoken in terms of Sankhya, here meaning knowledge of the self as distinct from the body. Now he turns to yoga, acting with the right understanding (buddhi). Scholars note that these words in the Gita do not simply mean the later philosophical schools of the same names.

A reassuring promise: on this path no effort is wasted and nothing goes into reverse. In many undertakings an unfinished effort is simply lost; here, even a little protects. Krishna returns to the idea in chapter 6, when Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and falls short.

Vyavasayatmika buddhi, "resolute understanding," is single and focused, while the thoughts of the irresolute branch out endlessly. Krishna is describing an inner unity of purpose. The one-pointed mind (ekagrata) becomes a central ideal in Indian meditation traditions.

The Gita's first mention of the three gunas, the qualities of nature: sattva (clarity), rajas (activity, passion) and tamas (inertia). Krishna places Vedic ritual done for worldly rewards within their realm and asks Arjuna to rise above them. Traditional commentators read this as moving beyond ritual for gain, not as rejecting the Vedas.

An image from village life: when floods cover the land, a small water tank adds little. Many commentators read it this way: for one who knows the self, whatever the Vedic rituals were meant to bring is already contained in that knowledge, as small reservoirs are in the flood.

Perhaps the most quoted verse of the Gita and the heart of karma yoga, the path of action. It has four parts: a right to action, no claim on its results, no acting for the sake of results, and no retreat into inaction. Gandhi named his Gujarati translation of the Gita Anasaktiyoga, "the yoga of non-attachment."

One of the Gita's best-known definitions of yoga, often quoted in Sanskrit as yogah karmasu kaushalam. The skill meant here is acting without being bound by results, so that neither good nor bad deeds tie one down. Buddhi, Besant's "Pure Reason," is the discerning intellect.

Arjuna asks a practical question: what is a person of steady wisdom, a sthitaprajna, actually like? How do they speak, sit and walk? Krishna's answer fills the rest of chapter 2, and Gandhi had these closing verses recited at the daily prayers of his ashram.

The first mark of the sthitaprajna: one who has let go of every craving of the mind and is content in the self alone. The happiness described comes from within, not from getting what one wants. Besant capitalises "Self" for the deeper self, the atman, as distinct from the everyday self.

The muni, or sage, of steady mind is neither shaken by sorrow nor hungry for pleasure, and is free of passion, fear and anger. The same three, raga, bhaya and krodha, appear together again in chapter 4. Muni is traditionally linked with mauna, contemplative silence.

A memorable image: the tortoise drawing in its limbs. The sthitaprajna can withdraw the senses from their objects at will, as a tortoise pulls in head and feet. Many teachers point out that a tortoise can also put them out again: the image is of mastery, not suppression.

Krishna is frank about how hard this is: even a wise person who is striving can be carried off by the senses. Pramathini, the word for the senses here, suggests something turbulent and violent. Arjuna makes the same complaint about the mind in chapter 6.

posts.display: Man, musing on the objects of sense, conceiveth an attachment to these; from attachment ariseth desire; from desire anger cometh forth.
posts.caption: One of the Gita's best-known passages traces a chain of cause and effect in the mind. It starts not with an action but with mere dwelling on objects of the senses, which breeds attachment, then desire, and then, when desire is thwarted, anger. The next verse completes the chain.

The chain continues downward: anger brings confusion, memory of what one has learned slips away, the discerning intellect (buddhi) is lost, and the person is ruined. Krishna's following verses describe the way back: moving among the things of the world without attraction or aversion, which leads to peace.

Without inner harmony, there is no clear understanding and no steady contemplation, and without these, no peace. The verse ends with a question that answers itself. Ayukta, "unharmonised," is the opposite of yukta, one joined in yoga.

Another image from everyday life: a ship driven off course by a gale. When the mind follows whichever sense is roaming, understanding is carried off the same way. The word for understanding here, prajna, is the one in sthitaprajna, "of steady wisdom."

A famous paradox. What the world is awake to, the sage treats as night, and what the world sleeps through, the sage is awake to. Commentators often read it as two kinds of attention: one alert to worldly pursuits, the other to the self. Samyami means one who is self-controlled.

Rivers pour into the ocean all year, yet it stays full and unmoved within its shores. Krishna uses the image for a person whose peace does not depend on satisfying each desire. The contrast at the end is pointed: kama-kami, "one who desires desires," does not find that peace.

The description of the steady sage closes simply: no cravings, no sense of "mine" (nirmama), no ego-sense (nirahankara). Ahankara, literally "I-maker," is the sense of being a separate doer, a key idea in later chapters. Peace, shanti, is the word Krishna keeps returning to.

Chapter 2 ends with brahmi sthiti, the state of Brahman, and brahma-nirvana, the peace of Brahman. Nirvana, literally "blowing out," is better known from Buddhism, and scholars have long discussed the shared term. That completes Arjuna's crisis and Krishna's first teaching. Thank you for reading along.
